hook: A 2024 study finds that 70-year-olds score far lower on a vocabulary test than 25-year-olds. A different team followed the same people from 25 to 70 and found almost no drop. Both teams are careful scientists. The difference is the design, and knowing why is a favorite exam question.

prereq.q: A researcher measures two variables as they occur and finds $r = .40$. What can she conclude?
options: The variables are related, but one may not cause the other
prereq.why: A correlation shows a relationship; without manipulation it cannot show cause.

prereq.q: What does an identical-twin study help researchers separate?
options: The roles of heredity and environment
prereq.why: Twins share genes to different degrees, which lets researchers compare heredity with environment.

figure.caption: Cross-sectional designs compare different age groups once; longitudinal designs follow one group over time.

chain.cause: A cross-sectional study compares different age groups at one time
chain.effect: each age group is also a different birth cohort

chain.cause: Cohorts grow up with different schooling, health care and technology
chain.effect: a difference between age groups can be a cohort effect, not aging

chain.cause: A longitudinal study follows the same people over years
chain.effect: it shows change within each person, but people drop out and the study takes years

chain.cause: Neither design can assign people to an age
chain.effect: neither one, alone, shows that age causes a change

ideas: Three themes frame every developmental question: nature and nurture (they interact), continuity and discontinuity (a ramp or a staircase), and stability and change (does a trait hold steady in a person?).
A cross-sectional study tests different age groups once: fast, but age is tangled with birth year, so watch for a cohort effect.
A longitudinal study tests the same people again and again: it shows change within people, but it is slow, costly and loses participants.
Age cannot be randomly assigned, so developmental designs describe and predict; they do not prove that age causes a change.

misconception.wrong: If 70-year-olds score lower than 25-year-olds in a cross-sectional study, the scores must fall with age.
misconception.right: The groups also differ in birth year. Some or all of the gap can be a cohort effect; a longitudinal study of the same people is needed to see change with age.

summary: Developmental psychology asks how people change and stay the same across life, framed by nature and nurture, continuity and discontinuity, and stability and change. Cross-sectional studies compare age groups at once and risk cohort effects; longitudinal studies follow the same people and risk dropout and long timelines. Neither assigns age, so neither alone shows cause.
